did_you_know.text: Did you know? In descriptions of sacrifices, the word “tamim” means an animal that is whole and without blemish. This emphasized that the offering was fit for sacred service.
Did you know? The verse lists three kinds of unleavened baked goods: bread, cakes, and wafers. Some were mixed with oil, while others were brushed with it.

Did you know? The ephod and the breastpiece were part of the high priest’s special clothing, not ordinary everyday garments. The Hebrew word related to the ephod is connected with fastening or binding.
Did you know? The expression “fill his hand” is a biblical idiom for appointing and authorizing someone for a role. It does not simply mean filling a hand physically.
Did you know? Placing hands on the animal’s head was a symbolic act of identification and dedication before the sacrifice.
Did you know? The “horns of the altar” were projections at its four corners. They were part of the altar’s structure, not the horns of an animal.
Did you know? Burning the sin offering outside the camp created a clear distinction between what took place within the sacred area and what was removed from it.
Did you know? Blood was placed on the priests’ right ear, hand, and foot. Some interpretations understand this as symbolizing listening, acting, and walking in sacred service.
Did you know? In this verse, blood and anointing oil together are connected with consecrating both the person and his clothing. The garments therefore become part of the dedication ceremony.
Did you know? The sacrifice is called the “ram of ordination” because of its connection to the expression “fill his hand,” meaning to authorize someone for priestly service.
Did you know? “Waving” was a ritual act in which an offering was lifted or moved before God. The word does not necessarily describe one specific motion.
Did you know? Portions of certain sacrifices were given to the priests. In this way, the priests’ service was supported through offerings brought by the Israelites.
Did you know? The seven days of wearing the sacred garments create a period of preparation and consecration before a new priest begins his service.
Did you know? Here, the word “tamid” describes a regular sacrifice repeated every day, not one offered continuously every moment.
Did you know? The Tent of Meeting is called by that name because it is the place where God meets or communicates with the Israelites.
